answer:
Recommendation: run a six-week, once-a-week "Make Something Real" programme for 13-to-17-year-olds built around a shared, visible project (a zine or small photo-and-text booklet, then a public showcase), with a paid-in-food and recognition structure, recruited through schools, youth groups and the teens' own peers rather than library posters, and measured with a short pre/post survey on reading confidence, library self-efficacy and intention to return, plus a weekly skills checklist and a six-week follow-up count of library card sign-ups and borrowing. This fits the constraints: one librarian at four hours a week and a $500 budget.

Why teens who do not read for pleasure would come: a reading-club pitch loses them before the door, so the hook is making something with a tangible output they can keep and show people. Each session runs for 90 minutes (weekly, so the librarian's time is 1.5 hours of facilitation plus 2.5 hours of preparation, outreach and admin, totalling four hours). Week 1 is an open "what do you care about" session with prompts, games and no writing required; week 2 introduces photo or drawing-based storytelling; week 3 teaches simple layout and editing on existing library computers and printers; week 4 is peer feedback in pairs; week 5 is production and printing; week 6 is a public showcase where families and staff attend and each teen receives a printed copy. Food at every session (pizza or snacks) and a certificate-free, peer-credited finish keep the social reward high. Librarians should not run it as a lesson; volunteers (ideally a couple of young adults or retired teachers, recruited via the local college or volunteer centre) sit with small groups.

Reaching teens who do not use the library: rather than advertising to the general public, go where teens already are. Contact the local secondary schools' counsellors and after-school coordinators to arrange referrals and a short talk in lunch or tutorial periods; approach youth clubs, sports clubs, faith groups and the youth justice or youth work service; and ask two or three teens recruited in the first week to bring a friend (a peer referral with a small thank-you). Visit the branch's own library-adjacent spaces such as the bus stop, skate park or high-street cafe with a one-page flyer that speaks about making a booklet, not about reading. Keep sign-up to a single QR code or text number and collect a parent or guardian consent form in person, so a teen can join with one step.

Budget of $500 across six weeks: printing and binding of the final booklets for up to 20 participants, including two proof copies per title and one spare, about $150; snacks and drinks for 20 people across six sessions plus the showcase, about $180; craft and stationery supplies such as paper, markers, sticky notes and glue, about $60; a small contingency for transport or a late printing fix, about $50; and a closing thank-you (vouchers for a local shop or a small book token for each completer), about $60. These figures are estimates and the manager should check local prices, but the point is that every line buys something a participant touches or eats, and nothing goes on the librarian's time, which the library already funds.

Outcome measures beyond attendance, all within six weeks: first, a pre and post survey completed in week 1 and week 6 using five-point scales on confidence reading and writing for pleasure, whether they see the library as a place for people like them, and their intention to borrow or attend again; because the sample is small, report the change for each person and the group median rather than claiming significance. Second, a simple weekly skills checklist (can they plan a page, edit a sentence, give peer feedback) completed by the librarian or volunteer, giving a visible progress trace. Third, behavioural follow-up at week 6 and again at week 10: how many took out a library card, how many borrowed an item, and how many returned unprompted. Fourth, a short exit conversation with each completer asking what they would tell a friend. Collect all of this on paper or a single shared form to keep the librarian's time within the four hours.

Caveats and open questions: a six-week programme with around 15 to 20 teens cannot prove a lasting effect, and the manager should treat the results as evidence of a promising change rather than proof; self-report surveys can overstate change, which is why the behavioural counts matter; the sample depends heavily on the referral partners, so the manager should ask which schools and youth services are willing to refer before committing; and the decision to repeat should also weigh whether the showcase drew new families into the branch. The main risk is that recruitment falls short, so set a minimum of eight committed teens before launch and have a fallback of a single session-based pilot rather than cancelling outright.
